article.title: React2STEAL Reused wfx-loot's Hijacked GitHub Accounts, GitGuardian Says, Echoing a GhostAction Overlap It Found a Week Earlier
article.summary: GitGuardian reports that React2STEAL's GitHub accounts also ran wfx-loot, and one ran PolinRider and GhostAction too, mirroring an account overlap it found between wfx-loot and GhostAction a week earlier.
article.body_markdown:
## Overview

React2STEAL is a campaign that runs GitHub Actions workflows from hijacked accounts to scan the internet for Next.js servers vulnerable to React2Shell, then publishes the credentials it steals into the same public GitHub repositories. [GitGuardian](https://blog.gitguardian.com/react2steal-hijacked-github-accounts-exploit-react2shell-and-publish-stolen-secrets/) reports that "On Nov. 18, OpenSourceMalware published research on a campaign it named React2STEAL," identifying "45 repositories across 44 GitHub accounts," and that "the GitHub accounts behind the campaign have also appeared in earlier attacks." GitGuardian calls it "a perfect storm of attackers leveraging multiple factors against their targets: the vulnerabilities have been known for many months, the attacker is using someone else's infrastructure, and the stolen credentials are available to anyone who finds the repositories." The specific earlier attack the accounts reappeared from, wfx-loot, is itself a campaign whose own account pool GitGuardian had already traced back to GhostAction a week before React2STEAL surfaced.

## Background

React2STEAL exploits two previously disclosed, already-patched flaws. [CVE-2025-55182](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-55182), nicknamed React2Shell, is described by the National Vulnerability Database as "a pre-authentication remote code execution vulnerability" in React Server Components "versions 19.0.0, 19.1.0, 19.1.1, and 19.2.0," with a CVSS base score of 10.0. [CVE-2025-29927](https://nvd.nist.gov/vuln/detail/CVE-2025-29927) is a Next.js middleware authorization bypass, scored 9.1, "fixed in 12.3.5, 13.5.9, 14.2.25, and 15.2.3," that lets a request carrying an `x-middleware-subrequest` header skip middleware checks, including authentication. GitGuardian notes that "patches for both have been available for months," but "they have not been universally applied, as this attack proves."

The campaign lands on top of a run of GitHub Actions-focused incidents the Herald has tracked since the fall. [GhostAction](/article/2026-10/10-stepsecurity-says-ghostaction-pushed-credential-stealing-workflows-to-345-repositories-via-two-hijacked-maintainer-accounts-on-october-8) pushed credential-stealing workflows into repositories in October using hijacked maintainer accounts. wfx-loot followed in November, using stolen GitHub credentials to push a CI secret stealer that [Aikido and StepSecurity](/article/2026-11/12-aikido-and-stepsecurity-say-stolen-github-credentials-have-been-used-since-november-10-to-push-the-wfx-ci-secret-stealer-their-counts-differ) separately measured at thousands of affected repositories. [PolinRider](/article/2026-09/18-polinrider-campaign-hits-packagist-planting-malware-in-a-700000-download-laravel-nova-package) is older still, first reported on Packagist in September. All three names now turn up again inside React2STEAL's own account pool, according to GitGuardian.

## Current situation

GitGuardian describes the attack chain as requiring minimal setup: "someone commits a list of target hostnames to a repository," which is "the full human interaction needed before firing off the workflow." A workflow named `scan.yml` then runs on a GitHub-hosted runner, where "a prefilter script that runs up to 400 concurrent requests to identify hosts likely running Next.js" operates, followed by "two exploit scanners" that each handle "250 targets at a time," trying "seven variants of React2Shell, the CVE-2025-29927 middleware header bypass, and a server-side request forgery through `/_next/image` that attempts to retrieve AWS role credentials from the instance metadata service." When an exploit succeeds, GitGuardian says a follow-on script "collects environment variables, cloud and Kubernetes credentials, and network details," with some variants also grabbing ".env and config files, collecting up to 300 KB per victim" and testing any AI provider keys found, which GitGuardian says helps "make them harder to distinguish from normal server traffic." The results are "saved on the runner as plaintext, JSON, and ZIP files" and committed into the same public repository rather than sent to an external server; GitGuardian notes a hard-coded Telegram bot exists in one script "but its sending function is disabled."

By GitGuardian's count, "live repositories were found to hold 1,281 unique victim hostnames across roughly 1,100 domains," and "a snapshot of 11 repositories contained about 9,100 ZIP archives, 3,800 JSON files, and 3,000 plaintext records, totaling roughly 7.4 GB of stolen data." "Researchers consider those numbers a minimum," GitGuardian adds. As of November 17, "new results were still being committed about every 11 minutes." Because the exfiltration channel is a public GitHub repository rather than a private server, GitGuardian warns that "database URLs, Stripe keys, and AWS credentials stolen from one victim can now be accessed by other attackers who know where and what to look for," and that deleting the repository "doesn't undo the exposure," since OpenSourceMalware found copies could persist in "forks, clones, and scrapers."

The account-reuse finding sits in its own section of GitGuardian's report: "a full 25 React2STEAL repositories the OpenSourceMalware team reported on contain the same probe file that wfx-loot used before deploying its stealer," and "one account was also known to be involved in the PolinRider and GhostAction campaigns." GitGuardian's FAQ states the limit of what this shows plainly: "OpenSourceMalware found that some of the same GitHub accounts were used in both campaigns. Whether the same operator is responsible remains unknown."

This is not the first time GitGuardian has reported this pattern. [Its November 13 report on wfx-loot](https://blog.gitguardian.com/wfx-loot-a-ci-secret-stealer-pushed-with-stolen-github-credentials/), drawn from "28,500 payload patches" across "2,367 accounts" and "17,715" repositories, found that "431 of the accounts used in the wfx campaign, about 20%, were already compromised in the GhostAction wave," and that in several of those repositories "the GhostAction security-audit.yml workflow still ran successfully on the wfx commits." That report also noted GhostAction had separately resurfaced on its own, "modifying 92 workflows left behind from previous waves," with only "16% (124)" of affected repositories "effectively cleaned up" by early October.

## Implications

GitGuardian frames the recurring overlap as evidence about the credentials themselves rather than about who is running any particular campaign: "this is a growing pool of compromised accounts that attackers can potentially use again and again at their convenience," and incomplete cleanup after GhostAction and wfx-loot "leaves the door open for further abuse." Its wfx-loot report offers an explanation consistent with that framing rather than a confirmed one: "the GitHub credentials used to push wfx-loot are not exclusive to its operator," drawing a parallel to GhostAction's own victim accounts, which GitGuardian says "were also used for unrelated cryptomining." Both of GitGuardian's reports stop short of attributing React2STEAL, wfx-loot, GhostAction or PolinRider to a single operator, or explaining how any of the credentials were originally obtained.

GitGuardian frames React2STEAL as part of a broader shift toward attacking credentials wherever they live — not just in source code, but across servers, developer endpoints, collaboration tools and CI pipelines — and cites its own State of Secrets Sprawl 2026 research finding that "28% of secret incidents are discovered entirely outside code repositories." Its recommended response treats patching as necessary but insufficient: "Patch React and Next.js right now," strip or reject the `x-middleware-subrequest` header at the proxy or WAF in the meantime, enforce IMDSv2 against the metadata-service request forgery, and then — regardless of whether a server was hit — "revoke personal access tokens, OAuth and GitHub App grants, and SSH keys" on any GitHub account that shows signs of compromise. As GitGuardian puts it, patching the servers closes the entry point this particular campaign uses, but "React2STEAL is built from known issues and is not a brand new concept. It is just automation of the abuse of known vulnerabilities, unpatched servers, and GitHub accounts compromised in earlier campaigns."
